newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC papers over cracks ahead of summit.
newsitem.headline: APEC papers over cracks ahead of summit.

text.p: APEC ministers papered over differences on Saturday and announced a united stand over a U.S. plan to free trade in information technology.

The announcement kept U.S. officials happy but raised questions over the role of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum as it strives to create the world's largest free trade zone by 2020.

U.S. trade negotiators had hoped APEC would seize the initiative on freeing up trade in computers, memory chips and telecommunications equipment ahead of the first ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation in Singapore next month.
In the end, the foreign and trade ministers, preparing for a summit of leaders in Subic Bay on Monday, tossed the issue over to the WTO.

A declaration at the end of two days of ministerial talks "endorsed the efforts at WTO to conclude an information technology agreement by the Singapore ministerial conference and urged all other members of the WTO to work toward that end".
U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor and acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky hailed the declaration.
"We think the language of endorsement is not only adequate but helpful as well as supportive," Kantor told a news conference. "We are delighted with the result."
Barshefsky said: "This is a significant agreement because it is the first time APEC has taken a stand on a WTO issue."

However, back-room negotiations to cobble together the agreement exposed gaps between developed and developing nations over whether APEC should press its own trade agenda or remain a loosely-organised body moving ahead only on the basis of consensus.
It left blurred the outlines of what is intended as a free trade zone joining two billion people with 40 percent of global trade in countries from China to Chile and the United States.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad was lukewarm in his endorsement of the U.S. plan. "We will support it to the extent it doesn't hurt us," he told a news conference.

Amnesty International on Saturday added its voice to unprecedented dissent swirling around the meeting by accusing Asia-Pacific nations of trampling over the rights of the poor, women and migrant workers.

"We're for APEC if it brings about justice and greater prosperity for people... but we're against it if there's a whole lot of evils associated with it," said Ross Daniels, executive committee member of the London-based group.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin was one of the first world leaders to arrive on Saturday. He will be joined by U.S. President Bill Clinton, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and other leaders from Wellington past Papua New Guinea to Ottawa.

Attention was focused on a meeting on Sunday between Clinton and Jiang amid signs that Washington and Beijing were edging towards a new understanding after years of bickering over human rights, arms proliferation, Taiwan and trade.
The relationship between China, an emerging economic superpower, and the United States will shape the destiny of the Pacific into the next century.
A parallel forum of 450 of the region's top business executives boasted deals worth more than $2 billion were in the works.

Philippine President Fidel Ramos, wrenching his nation out of economic backwardness into the ranks of Asian tigers, is reaching out to transnational corporations to try to translate APEC's ambitious goals into action.

But in the run-up to the summit, to be held at the former U.S. naval base of Subic Bay north of Manila, hundreds of demonstrators took to the streets of Manila to denounce free economic exchanges across the Pacific as a threat to jobs and a ploy by rich businesses and nations to exploit the poor.
And there were concerns that leftwing groups might be planning terror attacks on U.S. nationals, including diplomats and journalists.

An anthem penned for the summit celebrates "a voice emerging of a new Asia Pacific". It goes on: "United by an ocean great, fervid ideals thrown to fate, to lead the next millennium, economies cooperate".
